title: Boy Scout Troop 62 - Gridfall
description: Scout Troop 62 of Gridfall, on a template a parent bought in 2007: a calendar that stops in June 2012, a merit badge counsellor list with phone numbers, the pancake breakfast accounts back to 2007, an Eagle Scout list, and a photo album in which not one picture comes up.

blocks.text: *** BOY SCOUT TROOP 62, GRIDFALL *** MEETINGS EVERY MONDAY 7:00 TO 8:30 PM *** PANCAKE BREAKFAST THE FIRST SATURDAY IN MARCH *** A BOY CAN COME ON ANY MONDAY AND DOES NOT HAVE TO TELEPHONE FIRST ***

blocks.caption: The troop on Depot Street, Memorial Day 2007, waiting for the fire trucks to go first. This picture sits in the same folder as this page, which is the only reason it still comes up.

blocks.body:
Troop 62 has met on Ellery Street in Gridfall since [b]1919[/b]. The charter organisation is Gridfall First Methodist Church and has always been the church, through three buildings and one name change.

We have [b]thirty one registered Scouts[/b] and eleven registered adults. Boys come to us from Cub Pack 62 in February and from the middle school the rest of the year, and about a third of the troop is from outside the borough, which means somebody's parent is driving in from Nye Mills on a Monday night in February.

We are Troop 62 because the council registered sixty two troops in 1919 and this one was the last on the list. That is the whole of where the number comes from and somebody asks about once a year.

[b]Every Monday, 7:00 to 8:30 PM[/b], in the fellowship hall at Gridfall First Methodist, 214 Ellery Street.

Use the [b]side door on Bellamy Street[/b], not the front. The front is locked at six and the man with that key is not in the building on a Monday.

Park in the church lot or along Bellamy. Do not park in the three spaces at the Ellery Street end, which belong to the funeral home next door and which they need on a Monday more often than you would think.

The committee meets the [b]first Monday[/b] at 6:15, before the boys arrive, in the room off the kitchen. Any parent may come and any parent is welcome to say something. Most do not and that is how it has always been.

We camp ten weekends a year and one week in the summer. We cook on wood and on propane and we eat what the patrol cooked, which is the lesson.

We run the [url=/pancakes]pancake breakfast[/url] in March, which is the whole of our fundraising and pays for the trailer, the propane, the tents and about half of what summer camp costs any boy whose family asks.

We walk in the Memorial Day parade and we put the flags on the graves at the church on the Saturday before. We collect food in November. We do the flag at the borough council meeting in January, which takes four minutes and which two boys are always nervous about.

The rest of it is advancement, and advancement is a boy and a man in a kitchen with a [url=/meritbadge]blue card[/url] and a book.

rows: elected, and you should talk to him first

blocks.body: The Senior Patrol Leader line is not a courtesy. If a boy wants to know what to bring to a campout he asks the SPL, not Ron and not me. Ron will send him back to the SPL and has done it in front of people.

I am [b]Gary Wenrich[/b]. I built this in September 2007 on a template I paid eleven dollars for, because the troop's notices were going out on paper in a boy's backpack and were arriving in the kitchen in March folded into eighths.

I am not a computer person. I sell insurance. Anything on here that is wrong is wrong because I typed it wrong, and the way to tell me is the [url=/guestbook]guestbook[/url] or Monday at seven.

The [url=/photos]photo album[/url] does not work. I know it does not work. There is a page about that.

blocks.body: [b]This page was last changed Tuesday 5 June 2012.[/b]

The counter came with the template. Ellen does not believe it and neither do I. There are not twenty one thousand people who need to know when we meet. It is staying on because I do not know how to take it off.

The committee sets this in August and again in January. I type it in after the committee meeting, which means it is right for about three weeks at a stretch.

[b]There is a meeting every Monday at 7:00 PM unless this page says otherwise.[/b] Holidays we do not meet. Snow we usually do meet, because the church is heated and everybody is already sick of the house.

A date in [b]bold[/b] is one where a parent has to do something: sign a form, drive, or hand over money by the Monday before.

These are the counsellors in this district who have said yes to us. Every one of them is registered with the council and every one of them has been asked by Ron whether he may put the telephone number on this page. Two said no and are not here; ask Ron for those.

[b]The order is: card first, telephone second.[/b] A boy gets a blue card signed by the Scoutmaster before he calls anybody. A counsellor who is rung up by a boy with no card will be polite about it and will then ring Ron, and Ron will be less polite about it.

[list][*]The boy telephones, not the parent. The first time this happens he will be thirteen and it will be awful and that is the point of it.[*]Between [b]6:00 and 9:00 PM[/b] on a weekday unless the note says otherwise. Not at supper. Not after nine, ever.[*]He says his name, his troop, the badge, and asks when would suit. He does not say "I need to get this done by Friday."[*]Two people at every meeting. A boy does not meet a counsellor alone. Bring a friend working the same badge, or a parent, and the counsellor knows this rule already.[*]If a counsellor does not ring back in a week, ring once more, then tell Ron. Do not ring a third time.[/list]
Revised [b]14 November 2011[/b] against the district roster. Numbers in Ashkettle (619) and Coyne Flats (655) are long distance from a Gridfall phone, which the boys forget every single year.

blocks.body:
Railroading was counselled in this county for thirty years by a man in Marchfield who gave it up when the branch line closed in 2008. Three boys asked for it in 2009 and none since. There is a preservation group at [url=synth://verityrail-preservation.org/]verityrail-preservation.org[/url] and they have been asked and have not said yes or no.

For anything on that list, the council office in Marn County keeps the full counsellor book. It is paper, it is not on the internet, and you have to telephone them and ask them to read it to you. Ron does this about four times a year.

If you know a trade, a science, a craft or a sport well enough to show a boy, you can counsel it. There is a form, there is a background check, and there is no money in it.

We are short on [b]Aviation, Plumbing, Electronics, Public Speaking[/b] and anything to do with water. We are not short on Camping, because everybody's father thinks he counsels Camping.

Telephone Ron at 782-3841 or come on a Monday at seven.

blocks.text: *** SATURDAY 3 MARCH 2012 *** 7:00 AM TO 11:00 AM *** FELLOWSHIP HALL, 214 ELLERY STREET *** ADULTS $6, CHILDREN UNDER TEN $3, UNDER FIVE FREE *** EAT ALL YOU LIKE ***

blocks.caption: Doug Trostle at the two griddles, breakfast 2007. He has cooked the sausage every year since 1994 and has never once let anybody else do it. This picture is in the page folder and comes up; the ones on the album page do not.

blocks.body:
The first Saturday in March, every year since 1961. It is the only money this troop raises and it pays for everything the troop does that dues do not cover.

[b]7:00 to 11:00 AM[/b], fellowship hall, Gridfall First Methodist, 214 Ellery Street. Side door on Bellamy. Park along Bellamy or in the funeral home lot, which they let us have on that one Saturday and have let us have since 1978.

blocks.text: What it costs and what you get

head: PRICE
rows: Coffee to take with you, bring a cup
Coffee to take with you, our cup

blocks.body:
Pancakes until you stop, sausage, applesauce, orange juice, coffee, tea for two people who ask for it every year and who we now buy tea for on purpose.

[b]The syrup is the store kind and we do not say otherwise.[/b] We bought the real kind in 2009 because a committee member insisted, it cost seventy one dollars, nobody at any table remarked on it, and we have not bought it since. That is not a complaint about anybody. It is just what happened.

The butter is real butter. That one people do notice.

There are no tickets in the way people mean tickets. You pay at the door at the card table and Ellen Bixler makes change out of a cash box that has been the same cash box since before I was on the committee.

What a boy sells in advance is a [b]card[/b] that says he sold it, which he brings to the meeting on the Monday before, and which is how we know how many bags of mix to buy. Every boy is asked to sell eight. Nobody is made to and nobody has ever been sat down about it.

Advance cards are also at [url=synth://gridfalltire.com/]Gridfall Tire and Alignment[/url] on Depot Street and at the [url=synth://marchfield-coop.com/]Marchfield Farmers Cooperative[/url] counter, both of which have done this for years without being asked twice.

[b]6:15 AM[/b] boys arrive in the shirt. Two on the door, two on drinks, four in the dish pit, the rest carrying plates. A boy carries plates until he is fourteen and then he graduates to dishes, which he does not consider a promotion.

[b]Griddles[/b] are Doug and whoever Doug has decided is allowed near a griddle this year. [b]Batter[/b] is Barb Sechrist and three people from the church who are not scouting parents and never have been and who come anyway. [b]Money[/b] is Ellen and one other adult, always two, never one.

[b]11:00[/b] we stop cooking. [b]12:30[/b] the hall is back the way the church wants it, because there is a funeral lunch in it more Saturdays than not.

Ellen keeps this in the book and I type it in after the March committee meeting. Receipts are what went in the box, not profit. Costs run around a hundred and ninety dollars most years, and more the year we bought the syrup.

blocks.body: 2010 was the year we ran out of batter at twenty to ten and Barb sent two boys to the store on Mill Street for eleven pounds of mix, and we served it and nobody could tell. It is on the [url=/photos]album page[/url], or it would be.

[url=synth://ashkettlevfd.org/]Ashkettle Volunteer Fire Department[/url] runs a pancake breakfast in October. Ours is in March. This was worked out at a meeting in 1996 between three people standing in a car park and it has held ever since without anybody writing it down until now.

Go to theirs as well. They are nine miles out Route 62 and their hall is warmer than ours.

People send a cheque and they always have. Make it to [b]Boy Scout Troop 62[/b] and post it to the church at 214 Ellery Street, Gridfall. Ellen puts it in the book the same as cash.

We do not telephone anybody for money, we do not go door to door for money, and we do not sell anything except a plate of pancakes on one Saturday in March. If somebody rings your house saying they are raising funds for Troop 62, they are not.

[b]None of the pictures on this page come up.[/b] I know. Please read this before you sign the guestbook about it, because four people have.

The pictures are in a folder called album. The template put them there in 2007 and they came up fine for three years. On [b]19 October 2010[/b] the host moved everybody onto what the letter called the new system, and after that the pictures in the album folder stopped coming up for anybody but me.

They come up on my computer. That is the part I cannot get past. I have shown Ron. Ron says they come up on his too, and Ron's son says that is because we both have them saved on the machine already, and I think the son is right.

I have uploaded the whole folder again twice, once in November 2010 and once in February 2011. The host's help page says to check the file permissions. I do not know what a file permission is and the help telephone number on the letter has been answered by a recording in another state both times I have rung it.

What is below is the [b]description[/b] of each picture, which the template calls the alt text and which is stored in the page itself rather than in the album folder. That part still works. So the writing is here and the pictures are not.

blocks.text: Why the descriptions are as long as they are

blocks.body:
Barb Sechrist said in 2007 that a person using a reader for the blind gets nothing out of a photograph unless somebody has typed what is in it. Her brother is blind. So I typed what was in each one, and I kept doing it, and by now I have done it for about nine hundred pictures.

At the time it seemed like a lot of trouble for one man in Coyne Flats.

It has turned out to be the whole album.

head: FILE
WHAT IS IN THE PICTURE
rows: Nineteen boys and three adults on the dining hall steps at Camp Hoagland, Sunday afternoon, before anybody has unpacked. Everyone is in the shirt and everyone is squinting. Travis Kerchner is holding the troop flag upside down and does not know it yet.
The troop site under the pines. Eight canvas wall tents on platforms, two to a tent, and the patrol boxes stacked at the end of the row with the lids open to dry.
Austin Trostle at the waterfront in a life jacket, mid-air, about four feet off the dock, with his eyes shut.
Two boys at the rifle range benches with the range officer between them. Ear muffs on all three. The scoring paper is taped to a board behind them and it is not good.
Brandon Dinges' pot of what was supposed to be chilli, on the ground, on its side, in the dirt. This is the most requested photograph in the album and the reason is that Brandon requests it.
The whole camp at the flag pole for the Friday night campfire. Maybe two hundred boys. Ours are at the left edge and are half cut off because I did not step back far enough.
Ron Kerchner asleep in a camp chair outside the dining hall at two in the afternoon with a clipboard on his chest. Doug took this one.
Six boys and a leader in the water at the mile swim, taken from the dock, heads only, too far away to tell who is who. Logan Sechrist finished it. The picture does not prove that but he did.
The trading post counter. Four boys deciding how to spend nine dollars. This took eleven minutes.
A copperhead on the path to the shower house, photographed from further away than it looks. It was gone by the time the ranger came.
Cody Ebersole with his arm in a sling, grinning, on the Friday. He fell off nothing. He tripped on a tent stake in daylight.
The bus at the church lot on the Saturday, back home, boys asleep against the windows, and about nine parents standing in the lot with their arms folded.

head: FILE
WHAT IS IN THE PICTURE
rows: The sled at the starting line. Plywood, two-by-two runners, rope traces, and the number 62 in black paint that Marty put on the night before and which ran.
Eight boys pulling the sled uphill through about four inches of snow. Six are pulling. Two are pushing the back and are not really pushing.
The fire building station. A patrol crouched over a bundle of tinder with a fire steel. There is smoke in this picture and no flame.
The first aid station. A boy on his back in the snow playing the casualty, laughing, with three boys arguing over him about what a splint is.
Lunch. Boys sitting on the sled eating out of a pot. Somebody's mother sent brownies and they are gone in this picture.
The thermometer on the side of the dining hall reading nine degrees at half past nine in the morning.
Three troops' sleds lined up at the end of the day. Ours is the one with the rope splice in the middle of the trace, which happened at the second station.
Doug Trostle handing out hot chocolate from the back of his truck with the tailgate down. Eleven cups on the tailgate and a line.

head: FILE
WHAT IS IN THE PICTURE
rows: The gateway the boys lashed at the entrance to our site. Three poles, square lashings, and a cross bar with a board reading TROOP 62 GRIDFALL burned into it by Lloyd Kerchner.
Rain. The dining fly with eleven boys under it and the corner sagging with about a gallon of water in it that nobody has pushed up yet.
Zachary Gearhart cooking eggs in a pan on a wood fire, kneeling, with his sleeve about three inches from the flame.
The compass course flag in a hedgerow. This is what a compass course looks like and it is why boys say the compass course is boring.
The field off Herron Road in Cobb township, early morning, frost on the tents, and one boy up and walking around in a sleeping bag.
Six tents in the same field. The tree line behind is the Coyne Creek bottom.
A cook fire in a fire ring with a grate over it and two pots. Dylan Noll is holding a pot lid as a shield and is not being funny, the wind had turned.
Seven boys walking the old rail bed west of the Marchfield freight house. The rails are still in the ballast in this picture. The ballast is why we make them wear boots.
The trestle over Coyne Creek from the bank, fenced at both ends, taken from as close as we let anybody go.

blocks.body:
Seth Arbogast's Eagle project in 2011 was the troop's photograph box. Six hundred and eleven pictures, going back to a group photograph on the church steps that has 1931 on the back of it in pencil.

He scanned every one. He took the box to the Marchfield library on four Saturdays and sat with whoever would come and look, and he got a name on the back of a hundred and forty of them that did not have one. He wrote a description of each picture on a form and typed the forms.

The scans are on two compact discs. One is in the church safe. One is at my house on the shelf over the desk.

I have not put those six hundred and eleven on this page. There is no sense in adding six hundred more pictures that will not come up. I have the descriptions in a folder and if the album is ever fixed they go on in an afternoon.

Seth is at the state university now studying something to do with soil.
[i]If you know what a file permission is and you are in Gridfall on a Monday, the fellowship hall is on Ellery Street and I will buy you a coffee.[/i]

This list is on a plaque in the fellowship hall and it is on this page, and those are the only two places it exists. The council does not keep it by troop. The church does not have it in the minutes. I have asked both.

The plaque was repainted in 1988 by a man who did a careful job with the lettering and who worked from the plaque itself rather than from a list, because there was no list. [b]Four names were lost in the repainting.[/b] They were between 1934 and 1951 and we know they were there because two people remember reading them. Nobody remembers what they said.

Everything before 1962 on the plaque is a first initial and a surname with no year. I have not put those here because I would be guessing at the years, and a guess on a page like this becomes a fact in about four years. If you are one of those men or you are his family, ring me at 782-5290.

Years not listed below had none. The blanks are 1966, 1979, 1987 and 1995. There were five blanks on this page until April 2011, when a man in Halsey read it and rang me about 1970.

blocks.text: What an Eagle project actually is

blocks.body:
People think it is the building. It is not. It is the [b]asking[/b].

The boy finds somebody who needs something, gets them to say what they need in writing, works out what it costs, gets the money or the material donated, gets the permission, and then gets other people to come on a Saturday and do the work while he stands there and tells them what to do, which is the hardest part for a seventeen-year-old who has known these people all his life.

Brandon Dinges in 2008 is the one I tell people about. He spent five months on a foot bridge, got the drawing done, got the lumber promised, and the county highway department turned it down in one sentence because it was their ditch and their right of way and a foot bridge in it would be theirs to maintain for the next sixty years. They were right. He was sixteen and he took it well in the room and not so well in the car.

Then he built a shed. The shed took eleven days. The shed is behind the fellowship hall and the mower is in it.

blocks.text: If your name should be here

blocks.body:
Ring me at 782-5290 or sign the [url=/guestbook]guestbook[/url]. I have corrected this list four times since 2007 and every correction came from a man over sixty who found the page by accident.

There is a troop history page at [url=/history]the history page[/url] with the Scoutmasters on it, which has the same problem and worse.

A boy joins by [b]coming on a Monday at seven[/b]. He does not have to be signed up, he does not have to have a uniform, and nobody will telephone your house afterwards.

He can come three times before anybody asks you for anything. That is not a policy, it is just what we do, and it is because a boy who is dragged here by his mother in October is gone by November and a boy who comes on his own is here for six years.

Eleven to seventeen. Ten if he has finished the fifth grade and has done the Arrow of Light with Cub Pack 62, which meets in the same hall on Wednesdays.

He turns eighteen and he is out, on the day, whatever he has half finished. This catches somebody every two or three years and there is nothing anybody can do about it, so start the Eagle work at fifteen and not at seventeen and a half.

head: WHAT
HOW MUCH
WHEN
rows: Due in November with the charter.
Collected at the meeting in a coffee can. Nobody chases it.
Once. Second hand ones are in the cupboard for nothing.
See below before you buy one.
Troop 62 neckerchief, ours, not the shop's.
Depends on the site. Food is in it.
The breakfast pays part of this for whoever asks.

blocks.body:
That is about a hundred and ten dollars in a year for a boy who goes to everything, not counting summer camp.

[b]If that is a problem, say so to Ron or to Barb and it stops being a problem.[/b] The breakfast money exists for this. It is handled by two people, it is not discussed at committee, it is not written in the book by name, and no boy has ever been told which of his friends were on it. That has been the arrangement since long before me and it is the one thing on this website I would ask you to believe.

The shirt, the neckerchief, and the sash once he has badges. Trousers are whatever he has, and in this troop that is jeans, and it has been jeans since the seventies.

[b]Do not buy a shirt for a boy who has been here twice.[/b] There is a cupboard in the hall with about forty shirts in it in every size, clean, hung up, free, and the only rule is that he takes the patches off properly if he grows out of it and puts it back.

Ron will tell you the same thing and he will tell you before you have finished asking.

Drives. That is most of it and there is no way around it, because the campouts are between eleven and forty miles away and the boys are eleven to seventeen.

Beyond that: come to the committee on the first Monday if you want to know how anything works. Come to the breakfast. Say yes once a year to something.

[b]You are not expected to camp.[/b] Four adults camp regularly in this troop and they have been doing it for a long time and they are not short of company. If you want to come out, come out, and somebody will lend you everything.

Anything that has a boy in it has two adults in it. Not one. This is not negotiable and it is not about anybody here.

Two: the registration, and the health form. The health form part A and B you fill in yourself. Part C needs a doctor and it is only for summer camp and for anything over seventy two hours.

[b]Get part C done in the spring.[/b] Every single year somebody rings Dr Frantz's office on the last Monday in June and every single year the answer is three weeks.

Forms are at the meeting on the table by the door, or ring Barb at 782-1174.

This troop is boys. The question gets asked about twice a year and it is a fair question and the answer is that the programme is what it is and I do not make the rules and neither does Ron.

There are Girl Scouts in Gridfall and they meet at the school on Thursdays. I do not have a number for them, which is a thing I should fix and have not.

This page exists because I was asked about boots eleven times in one winter.

We camp ten weekends a year and one week in July. The troop owns the tents, the stoves, the lanterns, the patrol boxes, the water cans, the dining flies and the trailer. A boy brings his own clothes, his own sleeping bag, his own boots and his own spoon.

[b]Nothing on this list has to be new and almost none of it has to be good.[/b] The only two things worth money are boots and a sleeping bag, and both of those turn up second hand.

items: Sleeping bag. Twenty degree or better for anything October to April. A summer bag with two blankets over it works and looks ridiculous and we do not care.
Foam pad or an inflatable one. Not nothing. The ground takes more heat out of a boy than the air does and this is the single thing new families get wrong.
Boots. Over the ankle, broken in, and waterproofed. Sneakers are how a boy spends Saturday night with wet feet and decides he hates camping.
Two pairs of wool socks per day. Not cotton. Wool or the synthetic kind.
Long trousers. Two pairs. One stays dry in the pack and he is not to touch it until Saturday night.
Layers on top: a shirt, a fleece or a wool jumper, a coat. Not one big coat.
Rain gear, top and bottom. A poncho does for summer. A poncho is useless in April wind.
Hat and gloves, October through April, and a second pair of gloves in January.
Mess kit: plate, bowl, cup, spoon. In a mesh bag with his name on it in marker.
Water bottle. Two in summer.
Torch, spare batteries, and his name on the torch.
Pocket knife, if he has his card. No card, no knife, and Ron checks.
Soap, toothbrush, towel, and the roll of paper from the bathroom at home that he thinks he will not need.
Rubbish bag for wet clothes. One bag. It ends up being three.
Anything with a screen. It goes in a box in Ron's truck on Friday night and comes back Sunday. This has been the rule since 2004 and the arguments about it stopped in about 2007.
Sweets, crisps, anything in a wrapper. Not because we are strict. Because of the mice, and because a boy who ate at eleven at night does not eat what his patrol cooked at seven in the morning.
An axe or a hatchet. Troop axes only and only at the wood yard.
Aerosols of any kind.
More than one knife, which somehow needs saying.

blocks.body:
One week in July at [b]Camp Hoagland[/b] in Marn County, which is the council camp and is about an hour and forty minutes on a school bus. We have gone there every year since 1958 except 1994 and 2002, when the bus fell through and enough parents drove.

[b]$215[/b] for the week if paid by the May committee meeting, more after. That is the camp's price and it includes the food and the programme. We do not add anything on top of it.

He will do four or five merit badges, of which two will be things he did not want and one will turn into something he does for the next ten years. He will come home filthy, sunburnt on one side of his neck, and will sleep until two on Sunday.

Visiting night is the Wednesday. Come. Bring nothing. Every year somebody brings a cooler and every year the ranger explains about the bears.

Four boxes, one per patrol, rebuilt in 2011 with metal corners Hank Ebersole made and would not charge for. Each box has: two pots, a frying pan, a griddle, a coffee pot, a spatula, a ladle, a can opener, a cutting board, washing-up bowls, soap, a scouring pad, matches in a jar, and a list of all of that taped inside the lid.

The list inside the lid is checked by the patrol quartermaster on the Monday after every campout. It is the single most ignored job in this troop and the reason we have eleven spatulas and one ladle.

head: WHERE
HOW FAR
NOTE
rows: September shakedown. New boys' first night out, eighty feet from a bathroom and a telephone.
A field and a creek bottom by the landowner's yearly permission. Ron asks in February and has never been told no.
Council camp. Camporee, Klondike, summer camp.
Canoe trip in August, water permitting. Two adults with a card.
The old rail bed, Marchfield end
Day hikes only, no camping. It is the railroad's ground and we ask each year.
One night in October with the astronomy club, whose site it is and whose rules they are. No white torches after dark, and they mean it.

blocks.body:
The rail bed hike is five miles from the Marchfield freight house lot west and back. The rails are still in the ballast and the ties are still down, and walking on ties is how a boy turns an ankle, so we walk beside them. The trestle at Coyne Creek is fenced at both ends and we look at it from the bank.

There is talk at the county about making a trail of it. There has been talk since about 2009. If it happens it will be a good thing for this troop and I will believe it when I am standing on it.

Chartered [b]1919[/b] to the Gridfall Methodist Episcopal Church, which became Gridfall First Methodist in 1939 and has been in three buildings on the same Ellery Street lot. The troop has never been chartered to anybody else and has never missed a year on the charter except 1943 to 1946, which is a gap in the council's book and not necessarily a gap in the troop.

What we have from 1919 to 1961 is two things: the plaque in the fellowship hall, and a cardboard box of photographs. Until 2011 most of the photographs had nothing on the back.

head: YEARS
NAME
NOTE
rows: The charter is in his hand.
First initial only. This is one of the things I would like corrected.
The council book has no charter for these years. Two men who were boys then say the troop met anyway, in the hall, without a registration, and they do not agree about who ran it.
Took the troop to Camp Hoagland the first year it opened and every year after.
Moved to the state capital for work and drove back on Mondays for eleven months before he gave it up.
Eagle 1984, this troop. Fourteen years as of this writing.

blocks.body:
[b]1931.[/b] The group photograph on the church steps with 1931 on the back in pencil, thirty one boys and four men. It is the oldest thing in the box. Seth Arbogast got names for nine of the thirty one in 2011 by taking it to the library and to the nursing home in Marchfield.

[b]1958.[/b] First year at Camp Hoagland. The troop went by truck. There is a photograph of the truck and nobody has ever identified whose it was.

[b]1961.[/b] First pancake breakfast. Fifty five plates. It was a Saturday in March because the hall was free on a Saturday in March, and that is the entire reason it is in March.

[b]1977.[/b] The troop's Christmas tree sale, which ran fourteen years and stopped in 1991 when the lot on Depot Street was sold. There is a ledger for it in the church office and it made more money than the breakfast does.

[b]1994.[/b] The June flood. The troop filled sandbags on Mill Street for two days. Tom Norris, who was the county surveyor then, has the proper account of that flood on [url=synth://tnorris.verity.net/]his page[/url] and it is worth reading, and I am not going to summarise it here badly when he has done it properly.

The substation at Depot and Quarry Road burned early on [b]Wednesday 11 June 2003[/b] and a large part of Gridfall had no power. The church was out from the Wednesday morning until the Saturday.

The meeting of Monday 16 June was cancelled. Ron rang round and then drove round, because the church's list was in the office and the office was dark and he could not read it. It took him an evening. Two families at the far end were out for five days and were not thinking about scouts, and he told them so and left.

Nobody died in that fire. Two Gridfall volunteer firemen were taken to County General for smoke and were home the same afternoon, and one of them was a cousin of Walt Pennock, who has counselled Electricity for this troop since 2005 and who does not discuss it. The state commission's report came out in November 2003 and said the cause was insulation degradation consistent with age.

I am writing that down here because a boy asked me at the breakfast in 2011 whether it was true that two men had been killed in it, and he had got that from somewhere, and I did not have an answer for him that I could point at. Now I do. It is also in the [url=synth://verityledger.com/]Ledger[/url] from that week and on the [url=synth://wiki.gridfall.net/]county wiki[/url].

The Blue Kestrel on Route 62 closed in [b]2006[/b] and the building has been empty since.

For about thirty years the troop stopped there on the way home from the Klondike Derby, cold and wet, and ate breakfast at eleven in the morning on a Sunday. We stop at the place on the Marchfield road now and it is fine and it is not the same and every adult in the truck says so every January.

Marion Teale's [url=synth://kestrel-journal.net/]kestrel journal[/url] has the menus and the photographs and who sat where. Two of the Klondike Sundays are on it, from 1988 and 1994, and our boys are in the background of one of them.

The troop's minutes from 1962 are in the church office in a filing cabinet, in folders, by year, and they are complete. Before 1962 there is nothing in writing that anybody has found.

If you have a photograph, a programme, a newspaper cutting or a handbook with a name in it, I will scan it and give it back the same week. 782-5290, or Monday at seven.
Local pages that are worth having. I check these about once a year and I have taken three off since 2007 because they stopped coming up.

head: SITE
WHY
rows: Their breakfast is in October and ours is in March. Their mutual aid page is the best written thing on the local internet and their address page is why Zachary Gearhart's project existed.
Rain and creek level. We read this the Thursday before any canoe trip and before the spring campout.
Ben and Marie Tosches counsel Astronomy and Bird Study. The October night on Perrin Hill is theirs and we are guests on it.
Ray Sabo's page about the road cut. Any boy doing Geology should read the measured section before he telephones.
Surveying, and the 1994 flood written up properly by the man who measured it.
Duane Sarbaugh counsels Automotive Maintenance and they take breakfast cards at the counter.
Same, and Gene Ostrander for the agriculture badges.
Where people in this county talk about this county. I do not post. I read it.
Nine people write it and it is right more often than anything else.
The paper. They have run the breakfast in the Saturday listings every year since 1961 without being asked.
The north end of the county. Two of our families are up there and this is how they hear anything.
Somebody's brother put four minutes of the 2007 breakfast on here. It is sideways for the first ninety seconds.
Burn permits, park permits, and the form for using a township road for a project.

blocks.body:
The ring went down at the end of February this year and came back around the middle of April. I telephoned nobody about it and as far as I can tell nobody telephoned anybody about it. It is a list of about forty local pages and it is the only way anybody finds any of them, and it was gone for six weeks and the sky did not fall.

We joined in 2007, the week after I put the page up, because it was the first thing anybody suggested.

Ask a question, tell us something is wrong on here, or say hello. I read it on Sundays.

[b]This is not how you reach anybody in a hurry.[/b] For anything to do with a boy on a campout, ring Ron at 782-3841. For anything at all urgent, ring 911. Somebody wrote in here about a lost sleeping bag in 2009 and I read it eleven days later.

Karen Fennimore, Marchfield Public Library.

A woman came to the desk on 11 August wanting the year her father made Eagle for a plaque the family is having made. The council could not tell her by telephone. This page could, and this page is the only place I have found that can, for any year after 1962.

I have printed all eleven pages of it and it is in the local history file under Gridfall, organisations. I have also written to Mr Wenrich at the Ellery Street address.

Two other things, for whoever reads this next. I telephoned the church. The troop still meets on Mondays at seven. There were nine boys in the hall the week I rang, and they have no website now, so this one is it. The breakfast was held on Saturday 7 March this year, adults eight dollars, and it is advertised on a sign at the Ellery and Bellamy corner and nowhere else at all.

And the compact disc from Seth Arbogast's 2011 project: the copy in the church safe will not read. The copy at Mr Wenrich's house does read, all 611 files, and I have a duplicate at the library. The disc has the scans. It does not have his descriptions. The descriptions are on the album page of this website, typed out under every photograph that will not load, and I have spent four Thursdays matching the two together. I am about a third of the way.

entries.author: VerityPulseAI
entries.body: Summary of this page: Boy Scout Troop 62 is a youth organization based in Gridfall, Verity County, that has been active since 1919 and is best known locally for its annual pancake breakfast, held each spring. The troop received regional attention following the 2004 substation fire, during which members assisted emergency responders at the scene. The organization continues to serve area families today. Residents interested in learning more are encouraged to contact local officials for current meeting times.
